pass_a_gloss: And it was possible then to see the mother of so many bearing with good soul, because of the hopes upon God, the toils and the deaths of the sons; for dews of piety and a spirit of holiness did not allow to be kindled in her entrails the motherly fire, the one also flaring up in many women as upon most grievous evils. And I suppose that I have set these things too beside, most useful toward the matter proposed, cutting them short from the writing; in order that we may see how much piety can do against the roughest toils and the heaviest tortures, and the love-charm toward God, being able to do more by excess than every love-charm. And with this love toward God human weakness does not share citizenship, being driven beyond the frontier from the whole soul and not able to work even by any amount, where there is the one able to say: my strength and my hymn is the Lord; and I am strong for all things in the one empowering me, Christ Jesus our Lord.
pass_b_english: Then one could see the mother of so many sons bearing the pains and the deaths of her sons “with good courage because of her hopes in God” (2 Maccabees 7:20). For dews of godliness and a breath of holiness did not let the mother's fire be kindled in her inmost being, the fire that blazes up in many women as at the heaviest of evils.

I think that I have set these things down too, abridging them from Scripture, as most useful for our subject, so that we may see how much power godliness has against the harshest pains and the heaviest tortures, and love for God, which is far stronger than every other love. Human weakness has no share in the citizenship of this love for God: it is driven out of the whole soul as an exile beyond the borders and cannot act even in the least degree, wherever there is someone able to say, “The Lord is my strength and my song” (Psalm 118:14), and “I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Christ Jesus our Lord” (Philippians 4:13; 1 Timothy 1:12).

choices.choice: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 27); the old English was a digest: it invented details not in the Greek ('seven sons perfected in one day', 'exhorted in a tongue the tyrant understood not', 'nursed seven martyrs unto heaven'), cited Exodus 15:2 where Koetschau names Psalm 118:14 (LXX 117:14), and dropped Origen's statement that he abridged this from Scripture to show the power of love for God, and the exile of human weakness from the soul.
'a breath of holiness', keeping the image of dew and cooling wind against fire (cf. Prayer of Azariah 27, which Koetschau notes).
